title: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse
subtitle: Caring for Adults with Confidence
intro: Program Outline Welcome to GNPS Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse. In international healthcare systems, adult medical-surgical nurses are expected to combine comprehensive assessment with clinical judgement, evidence-based care, structured escalation and effective multidisciplinary communication. This level bridges national nursing preparation with international expectations. It strengthens your ability to interpret trends, prioritise complex care, manage perioperative risks, communicate through structured handover and support culturally safe transitions between hospital and community care. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Apply internationally recognised adult-assessment frameworks Interpret clinical trends, laboratory results and diagnostic information Prioritise care for patients with multiple health problems Recognise and escalate deterioration using structured systems Manage common high-risk medical and postoperative complications Coordinate care with multidisciplinary teams Document assessment, intervention and evaluation clearly Plan safe discharge and continuity of care Deliver culturally responsive education and shared decision-making International practice requires nurses to move beyond completing tasks. They must explain why a patient is at risk, justify priorities, recognise when expected recovery is not occurring and communicate concerns clearly enough for others to act. By completing Level 2, you should be able to provide safe, evidence-informed and culturally responsive care for adults with increasingly complex medical and surgical needs in international healthcare environments.

sections.title: Advanced Assessment & Prioritisation in International Practice

content.text: International healthcare systems expect nurses to combine structured assessment tools with professional judgement. Adult patients may have multiple chronic illnesses, altered communication, polypharmacy and rapid changes in condition. Prioritisation must be based on risk, not convenience or routine.
Learning outcomes
Apply structured adult-assessment frameworks Prioritise care for patients with multiple problems
Interpret trends and diagnostic information in context Communicate urgent concerns using structured escalation

Structured Assessment Frameworks such as ABCDE help organise urgent assessment. A complete nursing assessment then explores system-specific, functional and psychosocial needs. Tools support consistency but do not replace clinical judgement.

Complexity and Comorbidity A patient may have heart failure, chronic kidney disease and diabetes simultaneously. Treatment for one condition may affect another. Nurses should identify interactions between disease, medication, fluid status, nutrition and function.

Priority Frameworks Airway, breathing, circulation, acute versus chronic, unstable versus stable and expected versus unexpected findings help determine urgency. New deterioration takes priority over routine care.

Escalation ISBAR or a similar framework communicates the situation, background, assessment and recommended action. Nurses should continue escalation if the response does not match the patient's urgency.

During handover, an IQN is told that an older patient is 'a little confused'. Assessment shows new confusion, fever, low oxygen saturation and reduced urine output. The nurse recognises possible sepsis, initiates the local deterioration pathway and communicates an urgent ISBAR rather than accepting confusion as age-related.
Key learning points
Use tools to support, not replace, judgement Consider interactions between multiple conditions
Prioritise new and unstable findings Escalate until an appropriate response occurs

Complex adult care requires nurses to anticipate complications, evaluate treatment response and coordinate multiple interventions. International practice emphasises evidence-based pathways, timely review and clear accountability.
Learning outcomes
Manage adults with complex medical needs Anticipate high-risk perioperative complications
Evaluate response to treatment Adapt care when expected recovery is not occurring

Respiratory and Cardiac Complexity Patients with combined cardiac and respiratory disease require careful oxygen, fluid and activity management. Breathlessness may have several causes, and the nurse should assess rather than assume.

Renal and Metabolic Risk Renal impairment affects fluid balance, electrolytes and medication clearance. Diabetes, fasting and acute illness can cause unstable glucose levels. Monitoring plans should reflect the patient's risk.

Perioperative Risk Older age, frailty, obesity, smoking, anticoagulation and multiple conditions increase surgical risk. Nurses should understand the purpose of prevention pathways and individualise care.

Failure to Progress Persistent pain, inability to mobilise, ongoing tachycardia, poor intake or delayed bowel function may signal complications. Expected postoperative findings should improve over time; worsening or unexpected patterns require review.

A postoperative patient remains tachycardic despite pain relief and develops abdominal distension with reduced urine output. The nurse reviews observations, fluid balance, wound and abdomen, recognises that recovery is not following the expected pattern and escalates for urgent surgical assessment.
Key learning points
Do not attribute all symptoms to one known diagnosis Adjust monitoring to individual risk
Compare recovery with the expected trajectory Escalate persistent or unexplained abnormalities

Adult medical-surgical care is delivered by multidisciplinary teams. Nurses coordinate information across professions and shifts, making accurate documentation and handover essential to continuity and safety.
Learning outcomes
Coordinate adult care with multidisciplinary teams Deliver concise and risk-focused handover
Document assessment, intervention and evaluation objectively Plan safe transfer and discharge

Interdisciplinary Collaboration Nurses work with medical staff, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, occupational therapists, social workers and community teams. Collaboration should be guided by the patient's goals and clearly defined responsibilities.

Clinical Handover Handover should highlight diagnosis, current condition, recent changes, risks, pending results, treatment response and required actions. A list of tasks without clinical meaning is insufficient.
Documentation Records should show assessment findings, clinical reasoning, action, escalation, response and ongoing plan. Objective language supports communication and legal accountability.

Transitions of Care Transfer and discharge are high-risk periods. Medication reconciliation, mobility needs, wound care, follow-up, equipment, transport and support at home should be addressed before the patient leaves.

An older patient is medically ready for discharge but lives alone and cannot safely manage stairs after surgery. The nurse raises the concern during the multidisciplinary meeting, coordinates physiotherapy and social work input, and documents the revised plan. Safe discharge is based on function, not only medical stability.
Key learning points
Coordinate care around the patient's goals Make current risks visible during handover
Document what changed and how you responded Assess function and support before discharge

Many adults live with chronic conditions that require daily decisions after discharge. Education should build the patient's confidence and ability to recognise deterioration, use treatments correctly and seek help early.
Learning outcomes
Assess health literacy and learning needs Provide culturally responsive disease education
Use shared decision-making and teach-back Support realistic self-management and follow-up
Individualised Education Teaching should reflect language, cognition, vision, hearing, cultural beliefs, finances and available support. Standard information may not meet individual needs.
Self-Monitoring Patients may need to monitor weight, blood pressure, blood glucose, breathing, wound changes or fluid intake. The nurse should explain what changes matter and what action to take.

Lifestyle and Treatment Adherence Diet, activity, smoking cessation, medication and follow-up plans should be negotiated realistically. Labelling a patient 'non-compliant' can hide barriers such as cost, side effects or misunderstanding.
Teach-Back Teach-back confirms whether the explanation was effective. The patient describes the plan in their own words or demonstrates a skill, allowing misunderstandings to be corrected.

A patient with COPD frequently returns to hospital. Through respectful discussion, the nurse learns that he cannot distinguish his preventer inhaler from his reliever. The nurse uses colour-coded written instructions, demonstration and teach-back, and arranges community follow-up.
Key learning points
Assess barriers before judging adherence Link education to the patient's daily life
Explain when and how to seek help Use teach-back to confirm understanding

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 4 - Level 2, you have strengthened your ability to assess complex adults, prioritise competing needs, manage perioperative risk, coordinate multidisciplinary care and support safe self-management. You are now prepared for Level 3, where the focus moves to leadership, systems improvement and global adult-health practice.
